IV. EXAMINATION OF RELEVANT LEGAL MATRIX 15.
The jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 397 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) is highly circumscribed.
The Court reiterated that its powers in criminal revision are limited and it cannot engage in re-evaluation of evidence.
In exercising its supervisory role, the High Court is justified in refraining from reassessing evidence to determine the correctness of concurrent findings made by the Magistrate and Sessions Judge.

The exercise of this power should be sparing, invoked only in cases of gross error, non-compliance with legal provisions, findings based on no evidence, or where material evidence has been disregarded, or judicial discretion has been exercised arbitrarily or perversely.
Consequently, the Court should exercise extreme caution in Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK interfering with orders framing charges and must not interfere without compelling grounds.

16. At this juncture, it would be apt to refer to the observations made by this Court in Amit Kapoor v.
Ramesh Chander and Another,1 explaining the scope of Section 397 Cr.P.C.

sentences.text:
Section 498A of the I.P.C. reads as follows:
"498A. Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty.

Whoever, being the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman, subjects such woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine.

Explanation-For the purpose of this section, "cruelty" means- (a) Any willful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health whether mental or physical) of the woman;
or (b) Harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her meet such demand."

21. In the light of the aforesaid language used in the Section, the provision would be applicable only to such a case where the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman subjects the said woman to cruelty.

When the ingredients of the aforesaid Section are present in a particular case, in that event the person concerned against whom the offence is alleged would be tried in accordance with law in a trial instituted Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK against him and if found guilty the accused would be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine.
22. The said section contains an explanation/ which defines "cruelty" as understood under Section 498A IPC.

In order to understand the meaning of the expression `cruelty' as envisaged under Section 498A, there must be such a conduct on the part of the husband or relatives of the husband of woman which is of such a nature as to cause the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health whether mental or physical of the woman.

23. Privy Council in Moonshee Bazloor Ruheem v. Shamsunnissa Begum,4 observed with regard to marital cruelty that:
"Indian law does not recognize various types of cruelty such as 'Muslim' cruelty/
'Christian' cruelty/ 'Jewish' cruelty/ and so on, and the test of cruelty is based on the universal and humanitarian standards, that is to say, conduct of the husband which would cause such bodily or mental pain as to endanger the wife's safety or health.

24. Now, Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code serves as a crucial legal framework aimed at protecting women from cruelty at the hands of 11 MIA 551 Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT,
CUTTACK their husbands and in-laws.

This provision is inclusive of all marital unions, whether Hindu or Muslim, affirming the principle that every woman deserves protection from domestic violence and harassment, irrespective of the religious context of her marriage.
The statute recognizes that cruelty can manifest in various forms, including emotional, financial, and physical abuse.

In cases where a husband or his relatives inflict harm or demand dowry, the applicability of 498A remains intact, reinforcing the legal standing that all forms of cruelty are unacceptable.
25.
The interpretation of 498A extends beyond traditional notions of marriage.
Even in Muslim marriages, where the concept of marriage may differ from Hindu customs, the essence of the law remains relevant.

The emphasis lies in the actions of the perpetrator; if a husband harasses his wife for money or engages in threatening behavior, including attempts on her life, it constitutes sufficient grounds for invoking this provision.

The law is designed to act swiftly in the face of such abuses,
ensuring that victims have recourse to legal remedies and protection, thereby encouraging them to speak out against their abusers.
26. Thus, the absence of a dowry system in Mohammedan marriages does not exempt them from the purview of Section 498A.
The law is concerned with the behavior of the husband and the impact of his actions on the wife, rather than the specific cultural practices surrounding marriage.
If a husband harasses or abuses his wife for financial gain, this behavior clearly falls within the definition of cruelty Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK as outlined in 498A.
The provision is designed to protect women from all forms of economic exploitation and emotional distress, regardless of the context of their marriage.

Therefore, when evidence of such harassment is presented, the legal framework allows for the imposition of 498A, affirming that financial coercion and abuse are serious offenses that warrant legal action, regardless of cultural or religious nuances.
27. Next, the counsel for the revisionist argued that the Nikahnama alone does not suffice to establish the existence of a marriage between the revisionist and the victim.
This attempt to undermine the validity of the marriage is a strategic but ultimately flawed position.

Even if one were to entertain doubts regarding the authenticity of the Nikahnama, the fact remains that the marriage was duly solemnized by the Qazi and corroborated by the testimonies of witnesses P.W. 6 and P.W.
7.
Their consistent and credible affirmations provide substantial evidence supporting the legitimacy of the marital union.

28. Furthermore, it is imperative to recognize that the legal framework surrounding marriage in Islam does not hinge solely on documentation but is reinforced by the solemnization process and witness testimonies.
The affirmation of the marriage by qualified individuals carries significant weight in legal contexts, thereby solidifying the revisionist's position as untenable.

Many High Courts have articulated that while a Muslim man may lawfully contract a second marriage, such actions frequently result in significant cruelty and hardship for the first wife.

The legal principle recognizes that the emotional and psychological toll on the first spouse can be profound, often leading to feelings of betrayal,
